messages.subject: Identifcation problem with a longitudinal configural invariance model using ordered-categorical data
parts:
Dear Lavaan community,

I have a little trouble identifying a configural invariance model for longitudinal measurement using orderded-categorical data with two time points. My goal is to identify the model in such a way that the unique factor variances are freely estimated so I can study unique factor invariance. In my current model, however, all unique factor variances are automatically fixed to 1 by Lavaan. Could you please help me find my error?

I used the recommendations by Liu et al (2017; http://psycnet.apa.org/buy/2016-25480-001) to achieve my goal:

1. At all measurement occasions, the latent intercepts are fixed to zero. 
2. At one measurement occasion (the reference measurement occasion, typically the first or last), the common factor mean is constrained to zero, and the unique
factor covariance matrix is constrained to be the identity matrix (Alternatively, the total variances of all latent responses at the reference measurement occasion can be constrained to 1.0, instead of constraining the unique variances to 1.00). At all other measurement occasions, the unique factor covariance matrix is a diagonal matrix with the diagonal elements freely estimated.
3. At all measurement occasions, the same observed measure is chosen as the marker variable, and the factor loading of the marker variable is constrained to be 1.00.
4. One threshold for each indicator (and a second threshold for the marker variable) is constrained to be equal across measurement occasions.

I think that my problem might have to do with not understanding the second recommendation fully. I constrained the common factor mean of the first time point to 0 with Voormeting ~ 0 and constrained the variance of time point 1 to 1 with Voormeting ~~ 1*Voormeting. The factor variances, however, remain fixed to 1. Below, you find my model specification. 

 

                                   model3 <- '

                                                           Voormeting =~ 1*V1 + V2 + V3 + V4 + V5 + V6 + V7 + V8 + V9 + V10 + V11 + V12 + V13 + V14 +

                                                                                    V15 + V16 + V17 + V18 + V19 + V20 + V21 + V22 + V23 + V24 + V25 + V26 + V27 + V28  

                                                           Nameting =~ 1*N1 + N2 + N3 + N4 + N5 + N6 + N7 + N8 + N9 + N10 + N11 + N12 + N13 + N14 +

                                                                                    N15 + N16 + N17 + N18 + N19 + N20 + N21 + N22 + N23 + N24 + N25 + N26 + N27 + N28

                                                           Voormeting ~~ Nameting

                                                           Voormeting ~~ 1*Voormeting

Dear Lavaan community,

I have a little trouble identifying a configural invariance model for longitudinal measurement using orderded-categorical data with two time points. My goal is to identify the model in such a way that the unique factor variances are freely estimated so I can study unique factor invariance. In my current model, however, all unique factor variances are automatically fixed to 1 by Lavaan. Could you please help me find my error?

I used the recommendations by Liu et al (2017; http://psycnet.apa.org/buy/2016-25480-001) to achieve my goal:

1. At all measurement occasions, the latent intercepts are fixed to zero. 
2. At one measurement occasion (the reference measurement occasion, typically the first or last), the common factor mean is constrained to zero, and the unique
factor covariance matrix is constrained to be the identity matrix (Alternatively, the total variances of all latent responses at the reference measurement occasion can be constrained to 1.0, instead of constraining the unique variances to 1.00). At all other measurement occasions, the unique factor covariance matrix is a diagonal matrix with the diagonal elements freely estimated.
3. At all measurement occasions, the same observed measure is chosen as the marker variable, and the factor loading of the marker variable is constrained to be 1.00.
4. One threshold for each indicator (and a second threshold for the marker variable) is constrained to be equal across measurement occasions.

I think that my problem might have to do with not understanding the second recommendation fully. I constrained the common factor mean of the first time point to 0 with Voormeting ~ 0 and constrained the variance of time point 1 to 1 with Voormeting ~~ 1*Voormeting. The factor variances, however, remain fixed to 1. Below, you find my model specification.

Hi Gerard,

first: Nameting ~ 1 looks fishy to me. Do you really want to set the factor mean to 1?

Otherwise, i have just some more general advice on how to tackle such a problem:

1. start with a simpler model, eg including only three indicators by factor
2. annotate each (cluster of) line(s) to make the model more comprehensible to yourself and others
3. specify all model relevant parameters: you can use NA to force parameters to be estimated

hth, felix

Hi Felix,

This is great! I didn't know about the NA specification, and now the model returns all I expected from it. Thank you so much!
Regarding the Nameting ~ 1, with this specification you are not setting the factor mean to 1, but let it estimate freely. If you want to set the variance to 1, the model specification would have been Nameting~1*1. See also http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/syntax1.html 

Kind regards,

messages.subject: Re: Identifcation problem with a longitudinal configural invariance model using ordered-categorical data
parts: My goal is to identify the model in such a way that the unique factor variances are freely estimated so I can study unique factor invariance.

Use parameterization="theta", not "delta" (i.e., fix unique variances to 1 instead of total variances to 1).  You are already doing this, but this explains why:

https://www.statmodel.com/download/webnotes/CatMGLong.pdf
In my current model, however, all unique factor variances are automatically fixed to 1 by Lavaan. Could you please help me find my error?

That is because software does not know when it is able to release identification constraints (fixing unique variances to 1) after equality constraints are imposed across occasions.  In the multigroup case, constraining thresholds would automatically allow unique variances to be freed in all but the first group.  But with a longitudinal model, you need to free those parameters manually in the syntax.
I used the recommendations by Liu et al (2017; http://psycnet.apa.org/buy/2016-25480-001) to achieve my goal:

That follows advice from Millsap & Tein's (2004) article on multigroup invariance.  I would read the much more thorough and recent extension of that research by Wu & Estabrook (2016):

https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11336-016-9506-0

Dear Terrence,

Many thanks for your answers. They have been really helpful in moving forward with my analyzes and understanding Lavaan.


Kind regards,


Gerard Flens



Op donderdag 5 april 2018 14:38:34 UTC+2 schreef Terrence Jorgensen:

My goal is to identify the model in such a way that the unique factor variances are freely estimated so I can study unique factor invariance.

Use parameterization="theta", not "delta" (i.e., fix unique variances to 1 instead of total variances to 1).  You are already doing this, but this explains why:

https://www.statmodel.com/download/webnotes/CatMGLong.pdf

In my current model, however, all unique factor variances are automatically fixed to 1 by Lavaan. Could you please help me find my error?

That is because software does not know when it is able to release identification constraints (fixing unique variances to 1) after equality constraints are imposed across occasions.  In the multigroup case, constraining thresholds would automatically allow unique variances to be freed in all but the first group.  But with a longitudinal model, you need to free those parameters manually in the syntax.

I used the recommendations by Liu et al (2017; http://psycnet.apa.org/buy/2016-25480-001) to achieve my goal:

That follows advice from Millsap & Tein's (2004) article on multigroup invariance.  I would read the much more thorough and recent extension of that research by Wu & Estabrook (2016):

https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11336-016-9506-0

Terrence D. Jorgensen
